clue.text: See 7
From religious studies, 'e's transferred into behavioural science

indicators.note: transferred says one letter of the word is carried to a new position within it

parts.note: the academic study of religion and God is theology
the clue names the letter e itself as the piece that shifts

explanation.surface: A scholar switches from religious studies into a behavioural science department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transferred' moves the E of THEOLOGY from third place to the front. The ''e's' looks like a dialect pronoun but simply names the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethology is the scientific study of animal behaviour, a branch of behavioural science.

clue.text: Portraitist left cathedral city

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, England

explanation.surface: A portrait painter leaves an English cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: ELY is a small English cathedral city near Cambridge; Sir Peter Lely was court painter to Charles II.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Peter Lely was a seventeenth-century court painter famed for his portraits.

clue.text: Much repeated statement from person paintings upset

parts.note: a man is a person

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the word for paintings is read bottom to top

parts.note: paintings collectively are art

explanation.surface: Someone keeps saying a phrase about a person whose paintings were knocked over.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'upset' means turned upside down, so the paintings word is read from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: A mantra is a word or phrase chanted over and over, as in meditation or a slogan.

clue.text: I start changing some US money in cultural area

annotationWithheld.why: I start changing some US money in cultural area: the wordplay (I START anagram + QUARTER) and definition cover ARTIST plus 13-across QUARTER, but the file does not group the two lights, so ARTIST alone has no definition
annotationWithheld.clue: I start changing some US money in cultural area

clue.text: Impressionist runs into Paris so wildly

indicators.note: into says the run letter is placed inside the shuffled letters
wildly says the letters of Paris and so are thrown into disorder

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: An Impressionist painter dashes madly into Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wildly' rearranges PARISSO; 'into' puts R inside it, giving PISSARRO. Camille Pissarro really did work in Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: Camille Pissarro was one of the founding painters of French Impressionism.

clue.text: So precentor converted section of abbey

indicators.note: converted means changed into another form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A choir leader has been converted to a new faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'converted' rearranges SO PRECENTOR. Poets' Corner is the part of Westminster Abbey where many writers are buried or commemorated.
explanation.definitionFit: Poets' Corner is the south transept of Westminster Abbey, holding memorials to writers.

clue.text: Painter of the cross, in his own words

parts.note: de la is French for of the, the painter's own language
croix is French for cross

explanation.surface: An artist of the Crucifixion describes himself in his own tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in his own words' tells you to translate into French, the painter's language: DE LA CROIX means 'of the cross'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugène Delacroix was a leading French Romantic painter.

clue.text: Writer of verses 12 revised

indicators.note: revised says the letters of that solution are reworked into a new order

parts.note: the number stands for the solution at 12-across, another poet

explanation.surface: A poet whose verses are a revised version of someone else's.
explanation.walkthrough: The solution to 12-across is rearranged ('revised'); 9 and 12 are mutual anagrams. Walter Savage Landor was an English poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter Savage Landor was a nineteenth-century English poet and prose author.

clue.text: Stop old disreputable practice of excluding outsiders from unions

definitions.text: practice of excluding outsiders from unions

parts.note: to end something is to stop it
gamy can mean racy or disreputable

explanation.surface: A call to end an old, disreputable custom of keeping marriages within the clan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unions' here are marriages, so the definition describes marrying only within one's own group.
explanation.definitionFit: Endogamy is the custom of marrying only within one's own tribe, caste or group.

clue.text: Long t-shirt son replaced

indicators.note: replaced means put back in another place, so that letter moves within the garment's name

explanation.surface: A long T-shirt that a son has swapped for another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective about the shirt; it is the verb 'to long'. 'replaced' moves S from second place to fifth.
explanation.definitionFit: To thirst for something is to crave or yearn for it.

clue.text: Writer of verses 9 revised

indicators.note: revised says the letters of that solution are reworked into a new order

parts.note: the number stands for the solution at 9-down, another poet

explanation.surface: A poet whose verses are a revised version of someone else's.
explanation.walkthrough: The solution to 9-down is rearranged ('revised'). Matthew Arnold was a Victorian poet and critic.
explanation.definitionFit: Matthew Arnold was a Victorian poet, author of 'Dover Beach'.

clue.text: See 5

annotationWithheld.why: See 5: second half of ARTIST QUARTER, but the file does not group 13-across with 5-down, so it has no clue of its own

clue.text: Parts of same issue raised together in courts

definitions.text: Parts of same issue raised together

explanation.surface: Pieces of one magazine edition are lifted together into law courts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'issue' means offspring, not a magazine number: four babies from one birth, brought up together.
explanation.definitionFit: Quadruplets are four siblings born at one birth; quadrangles are college courtyards, both shortened the same way.

clue.text: Thomas the Rhymer? (Not Hood)

parts.note: a rhymer named Thomas is a poet called Thomas; the bracket rules out the other Thomas who wrote verse, Thomas Hood

explanation.surface: A nod to the legendary Scottish seer, with a cheeky aside about a different Thomas.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas the Rhymer is a figure of Scottish legend, but here it means any poet named Thomas; Thomas Gray wrote the 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Gray was an eighteenth-century English poet, so he is a Thomas who rhymed.

clue.text: Changed order we'd otherwise put in writing

indicators.note: changed says the letters of the following words are altered into another arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone altered an order they would have written differently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changed' rearranges ORDER and WE'D (the apostrophe ignored).
explanation.definitionFit: Reworded text has been expressed again using different language.

clue.text: Enjoyed books by English novelist

parts.note: someone who enjoyed books read them

explanation.surface: A reader enjoyed books by an English novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Reade was a Victorian novelist, author of 'The Cloister and the Hearth'.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Reade was a nineteenth-century English writer of novels.

clue.text: Assemble machinery using this device

indicators.note: using says the letters are drawn out of the words that follow, which hold the run

explanation.surface: An instruction to put together machinery with a gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'device' looks like a gadget for the machinery, but it is the heraldic sense; the answer runs across 'assEMBLE Machinery'.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry a device is a symbol or badge, such as an emblem on a shield.

clue.text: Spots on TV author making name in broadcast

indicators.note: in says the abbreviation for name sits inside the word for scattering seed

parts.note: to broadcast seed is to sow it by scattering

explanation.surface: An author appears on TV, making a name through broadcasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots on TV' is a second definition (interference on screen); C P Snow was the author of 'The Two Cultures'.
explanation.definitionFit: C P Snow was an English novelist and scientist, author of the Strangers and Brothers sequence.

clue.text: Firmly restricting time, in impassive manner

indicators.note: restricting means hemming in, so the word for firmly closes around the letter for time

parts.note: something done firmly is done solidly

explanation.surface: Someone firmly keeps to schedule while staying expressionless.
explanation.definitionFit: To act stolidly is to show no emotion, calm and unexcitable.

clue.text: Silly bowler's trick that could hold up play, for example

definitions.text: that could hold up play, for example

indicators.note: silly suggests something foolish or mixed up, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A cricket bowler's daft time-wasting trick that might hold up the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly' looks like a cricket fielding position, and 'play' like the game; it is the anagram signal and a stage play that a stuck writer cannot finish.
explanation.definitionFit: A creative blockage can stop a dramatist finishing a script, delaying its staging.

clue.text: Where leaders are taking one, without success

indicators.note: taking means holding something within, so the phrase for the front closes around the numeral

parts.note: leaders are at the front, in the van
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Leaders taking one more try, but getting nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The van is the vanguard, the front of an army or procession.
explanation.definitionFit: Trying in vain means trying fruitlessly, with nothing gained.

clue.text: Standard charitable reason, ultimately, to make a subscription

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letters of the two words before it

parts.note: to subscribe in its old sense is to sign one's name at the foot of a document

explanation.surface: A charity's standard reason for getting people to sign up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'subscription' is taken literally: writing one's name underneath, which is to sign.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensign is a flag, and a standard is likewise a banner.

clue.text: Book with right tone, as edited for one in literary family

indicators.note: as edited means altered as an editor would, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An edited book with the right tone, written by a member of a famous literary family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as edited' rearranges TONE into ONTE. The Brontë sisters, Charlotte, Emily and Anne, were Victorian novelists.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlotte, Emily and Anne were the celebrated novelist sisters of Haworth.

clue.text: Material for roof that is put on church

indicators.note: put on, in a down clue, means placed above the next piece

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Roofing material that is laid on a church.
explanation.definitionFit: Straw or reeds bundled on a cottage top form a traditional covering.

clue.text: No lack of body in such wine?

definitions.text: No lack of body in such wine?

parts.words: No lack of body in such wine?
parts.note: a full-bodied wine is praised, but read literally the places holding plenty of bodies are burial plots, which also name a Bordeaux wine

explanation.surface: A wine buff praising the fullness of a red from Bordeaux.
explanation.walkthrough: 'body' looks like wine-tasting talk for richness; it is a corpse. Graves is a wine region of Bordeaux.
explanation.definitionFit: Graves is a Bordeaux wine district, and burial plots are where corpses lie.

clue.text: Producer of theatrical comedies, in general

explanation.surface: A playwright who was generally known for his stage comedies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in general' looks like 'on the whole'; 'in' is a link and 'general' is the US Civil War commander Philip Sheridan.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Brinsley Sheridan wrote 'The Rivals' and 'The School for Scandal'; Philip Sheridan was a Union army commander.

clue.text: Small fruit in little group of trees

parts.note: a haw is the red berry of the hawthorn

explanation.surface: A small piece of fruit found in a copse.
explanation.walkthrough: A shaw is an old word for a small wood or thicket; the theme also hints at the playwright George Bernard Shaw.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw is an archaic or dialect term for a thicket or small wood.

clue.text: Why enigma may be worked out by Nobel laureate

indicators.note: worked out suggests solving a puzzle, but here it means the letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A puzzle about why a Nobel prizewinner remains a mystery to be solved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be worked out' rearranges WHY ENIGMA. Ernest Hemingway won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest Hemingway received the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature.
